SEBoK Verification of System Requirements, Distilled

Fourth-batch SEBoK distillation, batch 4/5 (SE-147). The article-as-named is not a standalone SEBoK page; the canonical SEBoK surface is System Verification (Part 3 > Systems Engineering and Management, leads John Snoderly and Alan Faisandier) which subsumes verification of system requirements as the core scope. Verification is "the confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled." Cluster A universal-sibling lattice is the dominant structural form: the verification methods (inspection, analysis, demonstration, test, similarity/analogy) are universal-sibling lattice at the verification-method rung. The verification-versus-validation distinction ("solved the problem right" versus "working the right problem") reads as Doc 372 hypostatic-boundary discipline at the methodological rung: verification is binary-comparison, validation requires value-judgment. Cluster K V3-as-procedure-binding shows in the four-step process (planning, performing, analysis, control); Cluster B multi-keeper at the verification-evidence-acceptance rung.

II. Source Read

Verification: "the confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled." The process checks correctness of system elements, documents, requirements, and services throughout the lifecycle, identifying faults and defects introduced during transformation of inputs into outputs. Five methods: (1) Inspection (visual or dimensional examination using human senses or simple measurement without destructive testing); (2) Analysis ("technique based on analytical evidence obtained without any intervention on the submitted element using mathematical or probabilistic calculation"); (3) Demonstration (correct operation against observable characteristics with minimal instrumentation, sometimes called field testing); (4) Test ("functional, measurable characteristics, operability, supportability, or performance capability is quantitatively verified when subjected to controlled conditions"); (5) Similarity/Analogy (uses evidence from comparable elements when design, manufacture, use, and operational environments are equivalent). Verification-versus-validation distinction: verification ensures "one has solved the problem right" (binary comparison, individual elements); validation ensures "one is working the right problem" (value judgment, integrated systems). Four process activities: planning (scope, constraints, techniques, strategy); performing (actions, resources, procedures, results); analysis (results-vs-expectations comparison, compliance status); control (plan updates, stakeholder coordination). V-model placement: verification occurs throughout development in parallel with system definition and realization, continuing through deployment; integration, verification, and validation are processed together for optimization. Artifacts: verification plans and matrices; verification procedures; reports and change requests; issue/non-conformance reports. Lead authors John Snoderly and Alan Faisandier. Position: Part 3 > Systems Engineering and Management. Standards: ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2015, INCOSE SE Handbook, NASA SE Handbook.

III. Structural Read

Cluster A — Universal-sibling lattice (Doc 572 Appendix D), at the verification-method rung. The five verification methods (inspection, analysis, demonstration, test, similarity/analogy) are universal-sibling lattice at the verification-method rung. Each method binds every verification engagement universally as a candidate technique; the discriminator is aspect (sensory-direct vs. analytical-indirect vs. operational-demonstrative vs. controlled-quantitative vs. comparative-precedent), not rung-of-application. N=5 instance; this brings Cluster A's worked-example count to seven (six prior instances cataloged in SE-039 §VII.1 plus this one).

Cluster H — Hypostatic Boundary (Doc 372), at the methodological rung. The verification-versus-validation distinction is Doc 372 discipline operating at the methodological rung. Verification ("solved the problem right") describes a functional-correctness assertion the SE discipline can make about the engagement; validation ("working the right problem") describes a value-judgment the SE discipline cannot fully assert without keeper-side reference (the validation question requires reference to what the system is FOR, which crosses into purpose-territory the SE discipline keeps under hypostatic boundary). The clean split between binary-comparison (verification) and value-judgment (validation) is the methodological-rung instance of the Doc 372 discipline.

Cluster K — V3-as-procedure-binding (Doc 314). The four-step process (plan, perform, analyze, control) is V3 in procedural form against the rankism of "the engineer's word that it works is sufficient." The procedural binding requires (i) planning that pre-commits scope and method, (ii) performing that acquires resources and executes, (iii) analysis that compares results-to-expectations against pre-committed criteria, (iv) control that surfaces deltas back into plan-and-procedure. The procedure exists because verification-on-engineer-word systematically fails under schedule pressure; the binding institutionalizes V3. Cluster K instance count rises to 9.

Cluster B — Multi-keeper composition (Doc 604). The verification-evidence-acceptance pattern is multi-keeper: the verification engineer holds the evidence; the design engineer holds the requirement; the customer/authority holds the acceptance. Three-keeper minimum; the verification matrix is the formal reconciliation instrument. Adjacent to but distinct from SE-035's PM-SE risk-acceptance and SE-108's residual-risk-acceptance.

Cluster D — Ladder-extension (Doc 572). The V-model placement (verification throughout development, parallel with definition and realization) is ladder-extension to temporal-concurrency: each rung of the decomposition has a corresponding verification-rung that co-executes. Doc 572 Appendix C composes here naturally; verification is the canonical right-side of the V where the ladder's downward decomposition is mirrored by the upward verification.

Cluster F — Pulverization (Doc 445), in dual-mode. Verification planning is forward-pulverization (enumerate ways the system could fail to meet requirements and design tests to detect each). Verification analysis (results-vs-expectations) is backward-pulverization (decompose the evidence by requirement to verify each was met). Dual-mode at engagement scope, paralleling SE-108 Safety's dual-mode candidate.

VI. Provisional Refinements

Cluster A reaches seven worked-example instances. Six prior (requirement types, architecture views, competency dimensions, CMMI measures, MODA value axes, HSI domains, severity-probability) plus verification methods. Cluster A continues to be the densest cluster.

Cluster K reaches 9 instances. V3-as-procedure-binding load-bearing across nine domains; the synthesis successor is critically overdue. Aligns with V3-as-procedure-binding refinement formalization (sixteen formalized).

Cluster F dual-mode candidate strengthened. Verification planning (forward) and verification analysis (backward) are dual-mode within one engagement, paralleling SE-108 Safety's dual-mode candidate. Two independent dual-mode instances now; the dual-mode sub-form is ripe for formalization in Doc 445's next pass.

Doc 372 at methodological rung formalized. The verification-versus-validation distinction is the cleanest methodological-rung instance of Doc 372's hypostatic-boundary discipline; worth retaining as canonical worked example.
